title: Custom Memory: Placement new, Allocators and PMR
summary: `new` does two things: it obtains raw memory **and** constructs an object in it. The two can be separated. **Placement new**, or `std::construct_at`, constructs in memory you already have. Custom **allocators** and **PMR** (polymorphic memory resources) let containers draw their memory from arenas, pools or the stack.
ideas:
1. Count the allocations made in building a `std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string>` of 10,000 entries with a `CountingResource`. Add `reserve` and compare.
2. Time parsing a million words into a `std::vector<std::string>` and into a `std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string>` on a monotonic buffer.
3. Write a fixed-size block pool resource and use it with a `std::pmr::list`.

cards.a:
It constructs an object in existing memory, allocating nothing

`new (buffer) T{ ... }` only runs the constructor. You must later call the destructor yourself and release the memory separately.

cards.q: Why is a monotonic buffer so fast?
cards.a:
Allocating bumps a pointer, and freeing does nothing

It never tracks individual frees, which is perfect for short-lived bursts of allocations.

cards.q: Why can two `std::pmr::vector<int>` with different resources be passed to the same function?
cards.a:
The resource is a run-time pointer, not part of the type

Classic allocators are template arguments and change the type. A pmr container holds a `std::pmr::memory_resource*` instead.

cards.q: Why must a memory resource outlive the containers that use it?
cards.a:
The containers use it until they are destroyed themselves

Destroying the resource first leaves the containers with a dangling pointer for their final deallocation.
